doc.title: Donn Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 6, 2009

title: Joining the Catatonic Five as a freshman banjo player
summary: Arriving in 1954, Andre is recruited by Emerson Brown, rehearses at Paul Parker's house and joins the six-piece band.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Yes, I came to the hill in 1954 and I had had a little experience playing guitar and ukulele and banjo, just a bunch of kids hacking around, and I got up here and I was in Carnegie and I heard a banjo upstairs the first night and I went up and a kid was playing a tenor. And I said could I play it? And a fellow in the room said, “Hey, I gotta tell Emerson Brown about you.” Who is Emerson Brown? I didn't know and he said, “Well you know we have a jazz band here called the Catatonic Five.” And I said, “Oh, that's interesting.” So the next day Emerson showed up to my room and said, “How would you like to come down to Paul Parker’s house tomorrow for a rehearsal?” And I said fine. So I went down there and it was Paul Parker the art professor, rest his soul, playing piano, he was a barrel house Chicago-style player, and his son Mike on trumpet, and the other son, Larry, on bass, and a young fellow named Dick Sherman — not the Dick Sherman of today, but a kid from Clinton High School named Skooky Sherman. And so we started to play and said hey, I think we’ve got a banjo player. I said well that’s great because I’ve never really been in a band before. So from there on we started getting gigs and I went down to Utica to a hock shop and bought a really awful banjo, which I played. And then the college used us for a concert Friday night of winter carnival weekend, right after the basketball game and in the Class of ’55 yearbook in the page that says activities or entertainment or whatever, after, there is a two page photograph of the band on the stage in Commons.
Oh, how neat. So there were six or seven people in the band at that time?
At that point we had, let’s see Pete Ziefelt I think was playing piano, me and Emerson, so that makes three, Larry Parker — yeah there were six. Larry and Mike Parker and Skooky Sherman.
